Each post here uses a small, runnable experiment — linear probes,
activation patching, simple closed-form models — to ask one question
about how a language model represents some piece of the world. The
emphasis is on *cheap and direct*: every figure here reproduces on a
laptop CPU in under an hour.

The two themes so far:

**Numerical magnitude.** Small language models build a roughly
logarithmic axis for integer magnitude in their token embeddings. That
axis has direction-specific causal effect on multiplication predictions,
and the answer's log is linearly decodable from the residual stream right
before the LM head — but probing-vs-patching shows the probe direction
is correlational, not causal. Across three small models the behavioural
pull of the log axis on actual output is invariant at $\sim$22% of
"perfect" log readout.

**Physical scale.** GPT-2's bare-token embedding cleanly orders temporal
words (`nanosecond → millennium`) on a log axis but not length or mass
words — because length and mass tokens are semantically heterogeneous
("electron" is a particle first, a mass second). Contextualised probing
rescues both: with a `"the mass of a typical X is"` prompt, mass R² jumps
from 0.45 to 0.84. The model has the information; the bare token doesn't
store it on a probe-friendly direction.
